page_hint: Ch 12, §2 'Mental Model', para. 1 (page not determinable from chunk)
quoted_clause: The substrate is a set of bounded resources, and the architecture design problem is essentially a packing exercise.
observed: The mental model is introduced as a single packing metaphor, but the three gates are of three different kinds: memory fit is a capacity/packing constraint, throughput-at-SLO is a rate-and-latency constraint, and quality is an empirical constraint that packing cannot address. The very next sentence corrects this, so the reader's first-formed model is the weaker one.
evidence: Ch 12 §2, first two sentences: the second reads 'A candidate architecture is a valid packing of the workload's weight memory and KV cache into the available GPU memory, paired with a parallelism and caching strategy that delivers the required tokens-per-second throughput within the latency budget.'
root_cause: The metaphor was stated before the constraint taxonomy it summarizes.
correction: Lead with the taxonomy — 'the design problem is a constrained synthesis: one capacity constraint (memory fit), one rate-and-latency constraint (throughput at the SLO), and one empirical constraint (quality)' — and then note that the capacity constraint is the one that behaves like a packing problem. Keep 'packing' for the memory-fit gate only.
acceptance_test: A reader can state which of the three gates is a packing constraint and which are not, without re-reading.

page_hint: Ch 12, §2 'Mental Model', resource list (page not determinable from chunk)

page_hint: Ch 12 §4 (Measurement), item 3
quoted_clause: Tokens-per-second that a single device can sustain for prefill and decode, measured on the target hardware. This is the number that, multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout, must exceed the workload's tokens-per-second demand (92K input tokens/s average, 3K output tokens/s average, 368K input tokens/s peak, 12K output tokens/s peak).
observed: §4 instructs the reader to multiply a single device's token rate by the number of devices in the layout. §3 of the same chapter spends four sentences correcting exactly this error for the canonical layout: under TP=8 the host aggregate equals the per-GPU rate (~19,800 tok/s), not 8x it, because each GPU carries 1/8 of the FLOPs for the same shared token stream. The chapter therefore states the rule and its negation within ~1,500 words, and the §4 statement is the wrong one.
evidence: Re-derivation: 70B x 2 FLOP/param = 140 GFLOP/token full model. TP=8 -> 17.5 GFLOP/token/GPU. 989 TFLOP/s x 0.35 = 346.15 TFLOP/s effective per GPU. 346.15e12 / 17.5e9 = 19,780 tok/s per GPU; all 8 GPUs advance the same token stream, so the group rate is also 19,780 tok/s. Multiplying 19,780 by 8 (as §4 instructs) yields 158,240 tok/s, which is 8x the true host ceiling and would make the single host appear to pass the throughput gate by a factor of 8. The correct rule is: multiply by the number of independent replicas (data-parallel), not by the number of devices inside a tensor-parallel group.
root_cause: The device-multiplication rule was written for the data-parallel case and never qualified for the tensor-parallel case, even though §3 establishes the distinction explicitly and the whole chapter's host-count screens depend on it.
correction: Rewrite §4 item 3 to state the rule with its scope: 'A device rate may be multiplied by the number of devices only when those devices are independent replicas (data parallel). Inside a tensor-parallel group every device advances the same token stream with a fraction of the FLOPs, so the group's aggregate rate equals the per-device rate, not N times it. The screen is therefore: per-replica rate x number of replicas.' Add a one-line worked cross-check (17.5 GFLOP/token/GPU -> 19,780 tok/s -> host aggregate 19,780) so the rule and §3 cannot drift apart again.
acceptance_test: A reader who applies §4's rule to the canonical 8xH100 layout obtains 19,780 tok/s (not 158,240) and reproduces the ~5-host average prefill screen and the ~21-host peak KV screen. No sentence in Ch 12 or Ch 13 multiplies a per-device rate by a tensor-parallel group size.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (Worked Example), all three candidates; §4 item 3; Table 12-2 'Decode pool sizing' row
quoted_clause: 3. **Throughput per device** [ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2). Tokens-per-second that a single device can sustain for prefill and decode, measured on the target hardware.
observed: The chapter's own method requires a prefill AND a decode throughput number per device. The worked example derives only the prefill number (~19,780 tok/s for the 70B under TP=8; ~24,725 tok/s for the 7B on one H100). No decode rate is computed for any candidate. Table 12-2 has a 'Decode pool sizing' row that is filled with demand only for (b) ('decode pool sized to 3K tok/s avg / 12K tok/s peak'), with 'not sized separately' for (a), and 'not sized in this screen' for (c). Table 12-1's throughput cell for (a) says only 'decode BW-bound' with no number. The reader therefore cannot verify that decode is not the binding constraint, and the chapter's headline gate ('throughput at the SLO') is evaluated on half of the throughput it names.
evidence: Independent re-derivation of the missing decode screen (H100 SXM HBM3 = 3.35 TB/s): 70B FP16 decode reads 140 GB of weights per token step; under TP=8 each GPU reads 17.5 GB per step, so 3.35e12/17.5e9 = 191.4 tok/s per GPU and 191.4 tok/s per host at batch 1, multiplied by the batch (17 concurrent slots) = ~3,250 output tok/s per host at the canonical 17-slot occupancy. Demand is 3K avg / 12K peak, so decode is not binding for (a) at 21 hosts (~68K tok/s) or for (c) at 15 cards (7B: 14 GB weights -> 239 tok/s per card per step x ~46 KV slots x 15 cards = ~165K tok/s). The conclusion survives, but only because the reader performs an arithmetic the chapter never shows and never labels.
root_cause: The worked example was built around the prefill/compute screen (the harder and more novel number) and the decode half of the stated method was dropped rather than deferred with a pointer.
correction: Add the decode screen to §3 and to Table 12-2: state the per-host decode rate at the canonical concurrency (weights-read-amortized over the batch), compare it to 3K/12K tok/s, and fill the 'Decode pool sizing' row for (b) with a host count (decode-phase occupancy is 300 x 25 ms = 7.5 s of the 8.6 s service time, so the decode pool's in-flight population is 40 x 7.5 = 300 requests at peak -> ~18 hosts at 17 slots/host). If the decode screen is deliberately out of scope for this chapter, say so explicitly and cross-reference the chapter that owns it, rather than leaving a half-filled table row.
acceptance_test: Every candidate in Table 12-1 and Table 12-2 has a numeric decode capacity alongside its prefill capacity, and the reader can confirm from the table alone that decode does not bind at either the average or the peak.

page_hint: Ch 13 §3 'Escalating' vs Ch 13 §8 (mini-case)
quoted_clause: §3: 'the screen below is run at the average — at peak it reads ⌈400 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = 203 hosts at full utilization.'  §8: 'The architect's decision: escalate to the **cluster** tier but keep it on-prem — run a fleet of 8×H100 replicas behind a load balancer. With the canonical whole-slot KV/service-time screen (Ch 16/17), the fleet is ⌈100 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = **51 hosts at full utilization** — 73 working + 1 spare = **74 hosts** at Ch17's 70% target and N−1 rule on the u-only screen (ρ = 1), or 77 working + 1 spare = **78 hosts** at the Table 17-1 policy (u × ρ = 0.70 × 0.95 = 0.665) ... The result, with the 74-host headroom fleet (78 hosts at the Table 17-1 policy): p95 TTFT back under 1.8 s at 100 rps [ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO RESULT]
observed: The chapter's own escalation analysis computes the peak screen for the escalated workload (400 rps -> 203 hosts at full utilization) and then the mini-case, which is the chapter's capstone, presents 51/74/78 hosts as 'the fleet' and asserts a recovered SLO, without ever mentioning the 400 rps peak. The mini-case's stated result is therefore true only at average load and false at the peak the chapter itself derived. A reader who takes 78 hosts as the answer will re-saturate the service the moment the daily peak arrives.
evidence: Re-derivation: 78 hosts x (17 slots / 8.6 s) = 78 x 1.977 = 154 rps of capacity against the canonical 4x peak/average shape at 100 rps average = 400 rps peak. Oversubscription = 400/154 = 2.6x. The chapter's own §3 states the peak screen is 203 hosts at full utilization (400 x 8.6 / 17 = 202.35 -> 203), i.e. 203/78 = 2.6x the fleet the mini-case recommends. The mini-case's 'p95 TTFT back under 1.8 s at 100 rps' is a statement about average load only.
root_cause: The mini-case was written around the average-load screen and the peak screen computed in §3 was not carried into it; the mini-case therefore does not integrate the chapter's own reasoning, which is the specific failure mode the mini-case format exists to prevent.
correction: Add the peak to the mini-case: state that the 4x peak/average shape persists, that the peak screen reads 203 hosts at full utilization (and ~300+ under the Table 17-1 policy), and that the architect must either provision for the peak, shape it, or accept a peak SLO breach. Then qualify the 'p95 TTFT back under 1.8 s' result as an average-load result and add the peak-load SLO outcome. Alternatively, if the mini-case is deliberately an average-load scenario, say so and state the peak consequence explicitly.
acceptance_test: The mini-case states a fleet size, the load (average and peak) it serves, and the SLO outcome at both. A reader cannot leave the mini-case believing 78 hosts satisfies the escalated workload's peak.

page_hint: Ch 12 §8 (mini-case) vs Table 12-2 'Monthly fully loaded cost' row
quoted_clause: §8: 'The decision between Candidates (a) and (b) hinges on whether the doubled hardware cost of Candidate (b) is justified by its operational flexibility (e.g., independent scaling of prefill and decode pools, fault isolation).'  Table 12-2: 'not costed / not comparable — the ~21-host figure is the Ch 16 monolithic fleet screen; a two-pool deployment needs the ~19-host prefill pool + a decode pool + KV-transfer fabric, priced in a follow-up screen'
observed: The mini-case's central decision criterion is a cost ratio ('the doubled hardware cost of Candidate (b)') that the chapter explicitly declines to compute and defers to 'a follow-up screen' that the book does not provide. The chapter's headline architectural decision therefore rests on an unevidenced number, and the two statements contradict each other within the same chapter.
evidence: Independent re-derivation of the two-pool host count at the canonical peak, which the chapter could have done: prefill pool is compute-bound -> 368,000 / 19,780 = 18.6 -> 19 hosts. Decode pool is KV-resident for the decode phase only: decode duration = 300 tokens x 25 ms TPOT = 7.5 s, so in-flight decode population at 40 rps = 40 x 7.5 = 300 requests; at 17 slots/host -> 300/17 = 17.6 -> 18 hosts. Total ~37 hosts vs the monolithic 21 -> ~1.76x, not 2x, and the ratio is workload-shape dependent (it approaches 1x when decode is a small fraction of service time and 2x when decode dominates). The chapter's own framing (decode is 7.5 s of the 8.6 s service time) makes the ratio close to 2x, so the mini-case's claim is directionally right but is asserted rather than derived, and the true figure is not exactly 2x.
root_cause: The chapter treats the two-pool host count as a Ch 16 economics matter, but the host count is a capacity result that belongs to this chapter's own screens; only the dollar conversion belongs to Ch 16.
correction: Compute the two-pool host count in §3 (prefill pool from the compute screen, decode pool from the decode-phase KV occupancy screen) and state the resulting host ratio (approximately 1.8x at the canonical peak, with the reason it is not exactly 2x). Then the mini-case's 'doubled hardware cost' becomes a derived figure with a stated derivation, and Table 12-2's 'not costed' cell can be replaced by '~37 hosts (19 prefill + 18 decode) vs 21 monolithic; dollar conversion in Ch 16'.
acceptance_test: The 'doubled hardware cost' claim in the mini-case is traceable to a host-count derivation in §3 or Table 12-2, and the derivation states the workload-shape dependence of the ratio.

page_hint: Ch 12 §8 (mini-case), final paragraphs
quoted_clause: the architect's first return-to-synthesis move is to renegotiate the budget, shape peak demand, or revisit the model class. ... Its memory and economics are trivially favorable; its fate turns on that measured gate. Because candidate (c)'s quality gate is still open **[HYPOTHESIS]**, it is not a finalist — and it stays in the gate evaluation (Ch 14) rather than being excluded pre-measurement; the finalists are Candidates (a) and (b), and the near-term decision falls between them.
observed: The mini-case identifies the binding constraint (the $15,000 monthly budget, which the 21-host fleet exceeds by ~10.4x) and names 'revisit the model class' as one of the three return-to-synthesis moves. Candidate (c) IS the model-class revisit. Yet the mini-case then excludes (c) from the finalist set on the strength of an open quality gate, asserts that (c)'s economics are 'trivially favorable' without a number, and declares that the decision falls between (a) and (b) — two candidates whose own economics fail the budget by 10.4x and 15.5x. The chapter's conclusion therefore excludes the only candidate that could plausibly satisfy the binding constraint, on a gate that is not the binding constraint.
evidence: Independent re-derivation from the chapter's own totals: the self-host per-host monthly cost is recoverable from the two stated totals (21 x X + $10,000 staff = $155,816.93 -> X = $6,943.66/host/mo; cross-check 32 x $6,943.66 + $10,000 = $232,197, matching the stated $232.2K). At $6,943.66/host/mo, candidate (c)'s own screen (~4 H100 cards at average, ~15 at peak) is roughly 15 x (single-card monthly cost) and is plausibly inside the $15,000 budget, whereas (a) at 21 hosts is $155.8K and (b) at ~37 hosts is ~$267K. The chapter never performs this comparison, so the reader cannot see that the budget constraint may be satisfiable only by (c).
root_cause: The mini-case applies the three gates in the order they were defined (memory, throughput, quality) and stops at the first open gate, instead of ranking the gates by which one is actually binding for this stakeholder.
correction: In the mini-case, compute candidate (c)'s monthly cost against the $15,000 budget using the same per-host cost basis the chapter already uses for (a) and (b), and state the result. Then state the conclusion that follows: the binding constraint is economic, not quality, so the quality gate on (c) is worth running first because it is the only candidate whose economics could clear the budget. If (c) is still excluded, the chapter must say why the budget cannot be met by any candidate and what the architect presents to the stakeholder.
acceptance_test: The mini-case states a monthly cost for each of (a), (b), and (c) on a common basis and identifies which candidates clear the $15,000 budget. The stated finalist set is consistent with that comparison.

page_hint: Ch 13 §6 (Architecture Consequence), Fig 13.1 caption; vs Ch 13 §2 (Mental Model)
quoted_clause: Fig 13.1 caption: 'de-escalation (blue) fires on data-residency/sovereignty, on-device requirements, and cost — but scale-down decisions should also reference **utilization** (sustained low load on a tier), **failure domain** (a smaller tier has a smaller blast radius), **operations burden** (fewer hosts to run), and **SLO margin** (headroom to absorb a burst without breaching the SLO). Make these measurable: thresholds are examples to calibrate to your SLO headroom policy, e.g. de-escalate when 30-day p95 utilization < 40% AND SLO headroom ≥ 2× (30-day p95 TTFT ≤ half the SLO) AND the smaller tier's failure domain is acceptable.'  §2: '**Distance / geography**: SLO can't be met because the users are too far from the serving site → move the serving edge closer or add regional replicas (a *placement* move, not a climb — it belongs with the de-escalation moves in Fig 13.1).'
observed: The figure caption carries roughly 150 words of de-escalation policy, including four named criteria and a concrete numeric threshold rule (30-day p95 utilization < 40% AND SLO headroom >= 2x AND acceptable failure domain), none of which appears anywhere in the chapter's body. Simultaneously, the body's §2 explicitly assigns the geography trigger to 'the de-escalation moves in Fig 13.1', but the caption's de-escalation list does not include geography; and the caption's escalation list ('demand, KV residency, or goodput') omits the body's Memory trigger ('model + KV no longer fits one node -> cluster'). The caption and the body describe different figures.
evidence: Text comparison: §2's escalation triggers are Memory, KV residency per GPU, Traffic, Contention/phase interference, Distance/geography. The caption's escalation triggers are demand, KV residency, goodput. §2's de-escalation content is geography only; the caption's is data-residency, on-device, cost, utilization, failure domain, operations burden, SLO margin. Cost appears only in the caption; geography appears only in the body. The caption also asserts a threshold policy with no derivation and no label beyond the figure's [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual] tag, which covers the diagram but not a policy rule.
root_cause: The caption was used as a convenient place to park policy prose that had no home in the body, and the figure was then drawn from a trigger list that drifted from the chapter's own §2 list.
correction: Move the de-escalation criteria and the threshold example into §2 (or a short §2 subsection) as body prose with their own evidence label, and reduce the caption to what a caption should do: name the diagram, state the reading order, and say what the reader should learn. Reconcile the trigger lists so that the caption's escalation and de-escalation sets match §2 exactly, including geography and the memory trigger. If the numeric threshold rule is retained, label it [ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic] in the body where it can be argued with, not only inside a caption.
acceptance_test: Every trigger named in the Fig 13.1 caption appears in §2, and every trigger in §2 appears in the caption; the caption is under ~60 words; the threshold policy appears in the body with an explicit evidence label.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3, Candidate (a)
quoted_clause: Candidate (a): single 8×H100 host with prefix caching (Ch. 11). This is the per-request-latency baseline — the single 8×H100 host that the early book (Ch 2, 4, 7, 8) establishes as meeting one request's latency SLO. It is *not* a capacity baseline: a lone host cannot carry the arrival rate ... so its throughput-gate failure below is expected
observed: The candidate is defined as 'a single 8×H100 host', but the throughput gate is then evaluated against a replicated fleet ('the gate closes only when the host class is replicated to ~5 hosts ... ~6 ... and ~21 at peak'). A candidate defined as one host can never pass a throughput gate that is evaluated on 21 hosts. The chapter's own verdict for (a) is therefore 'conditional finalist' with 'throughput open' — a candidate that fails a gate by construction, with the gate's verdict computed on a different object than the candidate.
evidence: Structural: §3's verdict for (a) is '✗ single-host capacity: needs ~5 hosts at average load ... ~19 at the 368K peak prefill screen' (Table 12-1) and 'throughput open' (Table 12-1 second table). §6 then advances (a) as a 'conditional finalist'. The object being gated (one host) and the object being scored (a replicated host class) are never reconciled.
root_cause: The chapter conflates two different design objects — a single-host latency baseline and a replicated host class — under one candidate label, then scores the gate on the second while describing the candidate as the first.
correction: Define candidate (a) explicitly as 'the 8xH100 host class, replicated to meet demand; a single instance is the per-request-latency baseline', and state that the throughput gate is evaluated at fleet level for all three candidates (a), (b), and (c) — with the per-instance latency gate evaluated on one host. Then the verdict language ('conditional finalist, throughput open') becomes meaningful: the open gate is the fleet-level throughput and SLO measurement, not a structural failure of the candidate.
acceptance_test: A reader can state, for each candidate, what object the memory gate, the throughput gate, and the quality gate are applied to, and no candidate is described as a single host while being scored as a fleet.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3, Candidate (b); §3 'Memory/residency arithmetic summary'; Table 12-1 (b) memory cell; §8
quoted_clause: Each pool therefore needs its own 8×H100 host (residency = 140 GB weights plus the pool's in-flight KV population — at the canonical per-host KV budget (640 − 140 weights − ~64 runtime ≈ 436 GB, Ch 7/17), 140 GB weights + 436 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB — exactly the pool, zero headroom; co-residency beyond the canonical KV budget requires reducing the KV allocation or adding memory; one request's 24 GB is not the pool's population).
observed: The same 436 GB KV population is applied to both pools, and 'zero headroom' is asserted for both. That is true only for the decode pool, which must hold the KV of every in-flight decode. The prefill pool holds KV only transiently for requests currently being prefilled (and hands it off), so its KV population is far smaller and it has substantial headroom. The chapter's own parenthetical ('one request's 24 GB is not the pool's population') shows the author is aware that pool populations differ, but the arithmetic then treats them as identical.
evidence: Independent re-derivation at the canonical peak: decode phase duration = 300 tokens x 25 ms TPOT = 7.5 s, so the decode pool's in-flight population = 40 rps x 7.5 s = 300 requests x 24.9 GB = 7.47 TB of KV, i.e. ~18 hosts at 17 slots/host. The prefill pool's in-flight population = 40 rps x (8.6 - 7.5) s = 44 requests x 24.9 GB = 1.1 TB, i.e. ~3 hosts of KV (and 19 hosts of compute). The two pools' KV populations differ by ~7x, so 'exactly the pool, zero headroom' is correct for the decode pool and wrong for the prefill pool.
root_cause: The canonical per-host KV budget (a capacity figure) was reused as a requirement figure for both pools, without distinguishing the phase in which KV is resident.
correction: Split the statement: the decode pool's requirement is 140 GB weights + up to 436 GB of resident decode KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB (zero headroom at the canonical budget); the prefill pool's requirement is 140 GB weights + a transient KV working set (bounded by the number of concurrent prefills, not by the decode population) + ~64 GB runtime, leaving the balance of the 436 GB as headroom. Update Table 12-1's (b) memory cell and the §3 summary accordingly.
acceptance_test: Table 12-1's (b) memory cell distinguishes the two pools' KV populations, and the 'zero headroom' claim is attached to the decode pool only.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3, Candidate (c)
quoted_clause: its throughput is a genuine strength (24,725 prefill tok/s per H100 vs the 70B's ~19,780 per GPU under TP=8 — ~1.25× per GPU, ~10× per host-equivalent; ~4 cards at average load, ~15 at peak, Table 12-2)
observed: The '~10x per host-equivalent' figure compares an 8-card 7B node (8 x 24,725 = 197,800 tok/s) against an 8-card 70B node (19,780 tok/s), but candidate (c)'s declared layout is one H100, not eight. Table 12-2 explicitly warns about exactly this ('the ~197K figure is the 8-GPU node, 8 x 24,725 ≈ 197,800, not this layout'), so the chapter knows the hazard and then states the unqualified 10x in the prose that a reader is most likely to remember.
evidence: Re-derivation: 24,725 / 19,780 = 1.25x (per GPU, correct). 8 x 24,725 / 19,780 = 10.0x (per 8-card node, but candidate (c) declares 1 card). A reader who takes '~10x per host-equivalent' as candidate (c)'s advantage over candidate (a) will believe a single H100 is 10x an 8xH100 host, which is false by a factor of 80.
root_cause: A comparison made for a hypothetical 8-card 7B node was carried into the candidate's own description without the layout qualifier that the table supplies.
correction: Either drop the '~10x per host-equivalent' clause from §3 (the 1.25x per-GPU figure plus the card counts in Table 12-2 carry the argument), or restate it as: '~1.25x per GPU; an 8-card 7B node would be ~10x an 8-card 70B node, but candidate (c) is declared as a single card, so its advantage is 1.25x per card and 4 cards at average load.'
acceptance_test: Every throughput ratio quoted for candidate (c) names the layout it applies to, and no ratio in §3 compares a 1-card layout against an 8-card layout without saying so.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3, Candidate (c)
quoted_clause: The 4-bit KV cache is a *memory* optimization, not a quality one; aggressive KV quantization can add its own quality penalty that must also be validated on the target workload.
observed: The two clauses joined by the semicolon contradict each other. 'Not a quality one' read literally means the change has no quality effect, which the second clause denies. The intended meaning is that the change is introduced for memory reasons and is not expected to improve quality — but as written the sentence licenses the inference that 4-bit KV is quality-neutral, which is exactly the inference the chapter's own §7 open question and §5 common mistake ('Using KV-quantization as a free lunch') exist to prevent.
evidence: Internal contradiction within one sentence; the same chapter's §5 states 'Quantizing the KV cache reduces memory footprint but introduces quality degradation that may be unacceptable for the target workload' and §7 lists 8-bit KV quality as an open [HYPOTHESIS].
root_cause: The clause was compressed to make the point that KV quantization is not a quality optimization, and the compression dropped the 'improvement' qualifier that distinguishes 'not introduced for quality reasons' from 'has no quality effect'.
correction: Rewrite: 'The 4-bit KV cache is introduced as a *memory* optimization, not as a quality improvement; it can nonetheless add its own quality penalty, which must be validated on the target workload.'
acceptance_test: No sentence in the book asserts or implies that KV quantization is quality-neutral; a reader who reads §3's sentence cannot conclude that 4-bit KV is free.
